Before it was
our home.

Albion’s story began elsewhere. Stoney Lane had witnessed two FA Cup wins, but by the end of the nineteenth century the club needed a new ground.

The new site stood beyond the town centre, on land associated with hawthorn bushes. It offered a fresh start. On 3 September 1900, The Hawthorns opened with a 1–1 draw against Derby County: Steve Bloomer scored the first goal, and Chippy Simmons replied for Albion.

What followed was a continual process of building, adapting and returning. The stands changed; the name stayed.

The club’s ground history ↗

A ground that
never stood still.

Selected moments in the building
and rebuilding of The Hawthorns.

  1. 1900

    The gates open.

    Four months of construction lead to Albion’s new home and an opening draw with Derby.

  2. 1913

    A permanent footing.

    Albion buy the freehold after initially holding a lease.

  3. 1920

    Concrete and champions.

    Concrete terracing arrives in the year Albion win the First Division.

  4. 1957

    Football under lights.

    The first match under the new floodlights is a 1–1 draw with Chelsea in September.

  5. 1964

    The Rainbow era.

    A new East Stand gains its familiar nickname from its brightly painted seats.

  6. 1979–82

    A new Halfords Lane side.

    The old stand is rebuilt in two phases.

  7. 1995

    A seated home.

    New stands replace the Birmingham Road and Smethwick End terracing.

  8. 2001

    The East Stand returns.

    The Rainbow gives way to a new stand, with club offices, hospitality, a shop and a ticket office.

  9. 2008

    The West Stand renewed.

    The former Halfords Lane Stand reopens after a major refurbishment.

  10. 2025

    Hawthorns at The Hawthorns.

    Twenty hawthorn trees are planted for the stadium’s 125th anniversary.

Sources: club ground history, opening the East Stand and the return of the hawthorn trees.

Four stands.
One Hawthorns.

Choose a side of the ground
to explore its history.

A simple guide to the four sides, rather than a seating plan.

The Birmingham Road End

“The Brummie” carries one of the ground’s most familiar names. The former terracing was replaced as part of the move to an all-seater stadium, with the new stand completed in 1995.

The ground’s earlier history includes a different kind of reuse: material from the old Handsworth Stand was moved to help cover the Birmingham Road terracing when the Rainbow Stand was built.

Follow the stand’s development ↗

The West Stand

The Halfords Lane side was rebuilt between 1979 and 1982. It later underwent a substantial refurbishment, reopening as the West Stand in 2008.

That work included dressing rooms, dugouts, a tunnel, executive boxes and facilities for broadcasters: a reminder of how much of a ground’s life takes place behind its seats.

Read the club’s account ↗

The East Stand

The Rainbow Stand’s final match came on New Year’s Day 2001. Its replacement opened that August, with a league game against Grimsby Town.

The new stand did much more than complete the enclosure around the pitch. It brought together offices, hospitality, the ticket office and club shop, changing how The Hawthorns worked throughout the week.

Explore the East Stand story ↗

The Smethwick End

The Smethwick End was the other major part of the 1995 redevelopment, as the old terrace gave way to seats.

Together with the Birmingham Road End, it marked a change in how supporters experienced their home ground: familiar ends, reshaped for a new era of stadium design.

Read about the all-seater transition ↗

Did you know?

A home for throstles, too.

In June 2025, Albion planted 20 hawthorn trees at the stadium. The hope was to welcome nesting song thrushes — bringing the bird and branch of the crest together at the ground again.

Read the club’s tree-planting story ↗

Albion’s home is 551 feet above sea level.

The club historian describes The Hawthorns as England’s highest league ground. An elevated setting for a Saturday afternoon.

Read Dave Bowler’s introduction ↗

64,815 people filled the ground for Arsenal.

The club records that FA Cup crowd on 6 March 1937. It belongs to a very different stadium era from today’s seated ground.

The people
we bring with us.

At the gates of a king.

Jeff Astle’s memorial gates were unveiled on 11 July 2003. Their crowned number nine and cup-winning celebration make the entrance to the ground a place of remembrance as well as arrival.

Open the Astle Gates exhibit →

Bomber, outside the East Stand.

Tony Brown’s statue was unveiled in 2014. Albion’s record goalscorer and appearance maker has a permanent place near the ground, as well as in its record books.

The club’s statue announcement ↗

If these stands
could talk.

Some afternoons and evenings
stay with a ground forever.

23 March 1966

A trophy lifted at home.

Albion beat West Ham 4–1 at The Hawthorns, completing a 5–3 aggregate League Cup final win.

This page draws on the club’s ground history, Dave Bowler’s account of the move from Stoney Lane, the East Stand retrospective, club records, and the club’s 125th-anniversary facts. Photographs retain their credits alongside the images.

The throstle uses the club’s published monochrome artwork. Baggie Bird is a newly generated fan illustration, based on the club’s mascot photograph; it is not official club artwork. This remains an independent fan museum.
